title: The Accidental Cross Join (Missing Join Predicate)
description: An old-style comma join with no join predicate produces a Cartesian product (a No-Join-Predicate warning); add the join condition. Why it matters: a missing join condition (easy to introduce with old-style comma joins) can silently multiply a query's cost by orders of magnitude -- and sometimes return subtly wrong data too.
narrative:
## Scenario
A report pairs orders with customer names using the old comma-style join syntax. It returns wrong, wildly inflated numbers and runs far longer than it should — the query accidentally matches **every order against every customer**.

## Why it's slow
With `FROM Orders o, Customers c` and only a filter in the `WHERE`, there is **no predicate linking the two tables**. SQL Server has no choice but to produce a **Cartesian product**: all 20,000 orders × 500 customers = 10,000,000 combinations. The optimizer even flags this with a **`No Join Predicate`** warning (a yellow triangle on the join) — its way of saying "you almost certainly forgot a join condition."

## What to look for
- A **`NoJoinPredicate`** warning on the join operator (Nested Loops with no join predicate).
- Estimated/actual rows exploding to the product of both table sizes.

## The concept
Always relate the tables you join. Add the join condition — `o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId` — (ideally with the modern explicit `JOIN ... ON` syntax, which makes a forgotten predicate a syntax error). With the predicate in place and an index on `Orders.CustomerId`, each order matches its one customer and the cross product — and the warning — disappear.
startingQuery:
SELECT TOP (100) o.OrderId, o.Total, c.Name
FROM Orders o, Customers c
WHERE o.Total > 995
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
hints: The two tables in the FROM clause have no condition connecting them. What does that force the optimizer to do?
No join predicate = Cartesian product (every order paired with every customer), flagged with a NoJoinPredicate warning.
Relate the tables: add o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId (preferably with explicit JOIN ... ON syntax).
